speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
maintopic: ANNOUNCEMENT OF AGREEMENT BETWEEN CANADA AND HONDURAS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I aim pleased to inform the house that a trade agreement was signed today in Tegucigalpa between Canada and Honduras. This agreement was signed on behalf of Canada by Mr. H. A. Scott, Canadian ambassador to Cuba, the Dominican Republic and Haiti, and by Mr. Pedro Pineda Madrid, minister of finance of Honduras.
Copies of this agreement have been tabled for the information of hon. members.
This is the first trade agreement between Canada and Honduras. It will enter into force on July 18 for an initial period of one year and will continue in force thereafter until either country takes action to terminate it.
The agreement provides for the exchange of most - favoured - nation treatment with respect to customs duties and related matters. This will provide new opportunities for Canadian exports to Honduras. Under this agreement, for example, Canadian exports will now be subject to customs duties and charges no higher than those levied on goods from the United States, on the basis of the trade agreement between Honduras and the United States. Similarly, Honduran exports to Canada will now be subject to the mostfavoured-nation rates of the Canadian tariff rather than to the general tariff rates, as has been the case up to now.
Honduras has specifically reserved the right to participate in a customs union with other Central American countries as it did in the case of its trade agreement with the United States.
As a direct benefit of this agreement, Canadian exports of wheat flour, canned salmon and sardines, upper leather, rubber tires and other products will henceforth be able to compete in the Honduran market on the same terms as exports from the United States. Honduras is a small but valuable open dollar market with no import or exchange restrictions. Canada's exports in 1955 were about $588,000, while imports from Honduras amounted to $1-7 million, about 90 per cent of which consisted of bananas.
This trade agreement with Honduras is particularly notable in that it completes the Canadian structure of trade arrangements with Latin-American countries based upon the most-favoured-nation principle. Canada has already exchanged most-favoured-nation treatment with all the other countries of Latin America.

Mr. Chairman, there was some consideration of the estimates of the Department of Veterans Affairs on Friday last and today I should like to make a few comments on this particular department. I believe the time has come to reassess the position of Canadian veterans and their dependents and the legislation designed to help them. While that legislation was designed to help these Canadians in fact it goes much deeper because in effect it is to repay them for the sacrifices they made for this nation. This obligation started right after the first war and it will continue as long as any of these veterans or their dependents remain alive.
I am afraid there is a tendency today to forget that many of the problems affecting veterans are still very serious and require immediate action, and furthermore that there always will be such problems. The reasons for this tendency to forget and for the apparent lack of interest are several, and today I should like to point out one or two of them to the members of the committee.
The first is that the veterans of both world wars are getting up in years. The annual report of the department for the fiscal year ended March 31, 1955 shows that at that date -I am quoting from page 85-the average age of disability pensioners of the first world war was 65 [DOT] 22 years. That means that today

I was surprised to find that the average age of those pensioners was 42-27 years, which would bring that age today up to 43 or 44 years. The ranks of the men who served in the first war are growing very thin; many of them have joined their comrades who made the supreme sacrifice. The veterans of the second world war have been busy getting established and it is more difficult for them to be interested in and pay attention to the problems which arise in veterans affairs.
Another reason for this tendency to forget and this lack of interest in veterans' problems is I believe the amount of talk there is about the so-called veterans' charter. Time and again we hear in this house of the wonders of the veterans' charter which is considered to have pretty well settled all the problems ;hat will face the veteran for all time.
The actual fact is that veterans' legislation started back during the time of the first world war. I think the Pension Act was passed in 1919. The three main acts affecting the veterans of Canada are the Pension Act, the War Veterans Allowance Act and the Veterans' Land Act; a similar earlier act was known as the soldier settlement act. Those three foundation acts were in effect long before the so-called veterans' charter of 1946. What was done in 1946 and during one or two sessions preceding that year was simply to bring up to date that basic legislation and to add certain other statutes to meet conditions which were peculiar to the second world war. The veterans' charter was passed eleven years ago and it does not meet the problems which are now arising and will continue to arise in connection with veterans' affairs.
Actually there is a great need today for an attack on the problems of the veteran and his dependents with renewed vigour. Yet that has not been done. Let me point out, as did the minister in his opening discussion of his estimates on Friday, that there has been no legislation brought into this house during the present session by the Department of Veterans Affairs. There was an amendment to the Veterans Business and Professional Loans Act, but that was introduced by the Minister of Finance. In his remarks the other day the minister sought to excuse this situation by saying that there had been some resolutions presented at the dominion convention of the Canadian Legion held in Vancouver a few weeks ago and that there had not yet been time for the government to review these


suggestions. His remarks are to be found on page 5747 of Hansard. He said:
As hon. members know, the dominion convention of the Canadian Legion in session last month in Vancouver passed a number of resolutions concerned with proposed legislative amendments, and as soon as these recommendations are received by the government I can assure the committee they will receive the careful and thorough consideration of the government and the officials of my department.
That really was not a very good excuse for inaction, because as a matter of fact most of those resolutions were presented to the government when the dominion officers of the legion met the cabinet on November 10, 1955, in plenty of time to have them considered in the intervening months.
Then we still have the situation that the minister is only a half-time minister in so far as the Department of Veterans Affairs is concerned. He was named Postmaster General on November 8, 1955, and for those eight months has been carrying on as the minister of two important departments. I complained about this situation on January 23, when I made my first speech of this session. Other members have complained about it; veterans' organizations have made a similar complaint; but the Prime Minister has done nothing about relieving the present Minister of Veterans Affairs of his obligations as Postmaster General. The blame for this situation rests not on the shoulders of the minister but on the Prime Minister himself.
According to the report of the department, there are over 300,000 Canadians directly affected in that they receive either a pension or war veterans' allowance or have settled under the Veterans' Land Act. I do not know the exact number because there will be certain duplications: for example, a pensioner may also be receiving a war veterans' allowance or may also be settled under the Veterans' Land Act. But there are at least a quarter of a million Canadians who are directly affected by what is done by the Minister of Veterans Affairs, and surely that job, if it is to be done properly, is a fulltime job. The minister should be relieved of his obligation to act also as Postmaster General. The very fact that the Prime Minister allows this situation to continue shows that he for one is not very deeply concerned about these problems facing the Canadian veteran.
Then we have the continued refusal to set up a standing committee on veterans affairs. Year after year, requests have been made that that step be taken, but every time they

have been turned down. When we form a government, we certainly will have a fulltime Minister of Veterans Affairs and we certainly will have a standing committee on veterans affairs.

speakerposition: Postmaster General; Minister of Veterans Affairs
speechtext: Wishful thinking.

The setting up of such a committee would result in rectifying the mistakes in legislation and in administration much more quickly than is done under the present conditions. It would also result in keeping the veterans legislation up to date, and I think it would make things a great deal easier for the staff of the Department of Veterans Affairs because it would bring them much more closely in contact with the people whom they are serving.
However, these veterans' problems are not to be dealt with at all during the present year. What is the result of that failure to take any action? Let me instance the case of the veteran on war veterans' allowance who reaches 70 years of age this year, and do not forget that these recipients of war veterans' allowance are in great majority front-line troops of the first world war, men who served in the trenches. The veteran who reaches 70 this year does not get a full old-age security payment of $40 per month. At least, he may get the full old age security payment, but his war veterans' allowance will be cut down. His fellow Canadians who did not serve at all in the forces will get the $40 automatically, but not this front-line fighting soldier.
The reason why he will not get it is because of the low ceiling placed on the annual income he is allowed. If that ceiling were raised from $840 per year to $1,200 per year for the single veteran, and from $1,440 per year to $2,000 per year for the married veteran, as requested year in and year out by the great veterans' organizations of this country, then that situation to which I have referred would be met. This veteran would be able to get his full old-age security payment when he reaches 70, and the small pensioner who is under 70 would be able to retain his small pension and get the full war veterans' allowance.
It is obvious that the government knows that this situation is not right, because there are palliatives being used to partially meet the needs. For example, provision is made for certain earnings to be exempt from consideration, and they are called casual earnings. We were told last year that only a small percentage of the recipients of war veterans' allowance were able to earn anything at all, but there is this provision for casual earnings, which helps some of them.
Supply-Veterans Affairs
Then the government has set up what is known as a war veterans' allowance assistance fund. If a recipient of war veterans' allowance has no other income whatsoever, then he can get a hand-out up to a total of $10 per month, subject to a second means test. He has to take the first means test to qualify for a war veterans' allowance and then, to get any help from the assistance fund, he must take a second means test. I repeat that these are palliatives which help but do not actually meet the situation as it should be met. In effect they prove the need for raising the ceiling on annual income.
The Department of Finance in its wisdom has decided that $2,000 income should be exempt from taxation; in other words, that the family man requires that amount to exist and that he should not pay any tax on it. I suggest that the same ruling should be made with regard to the married recipient of war veterans allowance. It is a very good argument in support of raising this ceiling to the sum of $2,000 per year.
I think it will not be denied that the reason why these ceilings are kept so low is to keep the veteran in line with the recipient of social welfare, although the fact is that the payments made to the veteran are payments for services rendered for the greatest kind of services that any Canadian could render; they should be treated on that basis rather than regarded merely as social welfare measures.
There is another problem concerning war veterans allowance recipients which should be met. Most of these men are getting up in years and their health breaks down. In some cases they have to go to the southern states or to Mexico, some warmer climate, in order to stay alive, and when they do that they lose the war veterans allowance. It is only paid as long as they reside in Canada. There is provision for a short absence from Canada but if they change their residence to some country other than Canada then they lose the allowance. We have always been told that it is too hard for the department to figure out any way in which special provision could be made to meet these cases where the man's health has broken down as distinct from cases where he decides to move away for reasons other than health. I submit that this problem should have been met during the present session. Furthermore, I see no reason why the allowance should not be paid to a veteran who goes to live in another part of the commonwealth, whether or not he goes for health reasons. The same ruling should not apply in those cases as is used where veterans go to foreign lands.
So far as war veterans allowance is concerned, there is also a need to meet the

Supply-Veterans Affairs situation of widows of imperial veterans who did not live for a full period of 20 years in Canada. Other members have dealt with this matter, have explained it very fully and have urged that the situation be remedied. The fact is, as we all know, that when provision was made to help these imperial veterans we had in mind the group of imperials who came here up to and including the year 1930. However, instead of saying that any veterans who had come here by that time would be eligible the amendment when passed in 1950 or thereabouts based qualification on the ground of 20 years' residence. Of course that meant that if the veteran died say in 1945 his widow could not qualify because the veteran had not lived in Canada for 20 years. This has been a mistake in draftsmanship and yet the department has never been willing to remedy it. That should have been done this year without any further hardships being imposed on this particular group.
Then there is the Pension Act. I believe the time has come to write into that act a presumption that injury or disease occurred after enlistment. As it stands at the present time, a veteran who suffers a disability now often has a ruling made against him on the ground that the disability originated before he joined the forces. In the second world war particularly medical examinations on enlistment were very thorough, much more thorough, as we all know, than was the case in the first war. I believe that the pension commission stretches things very far when it rules that a disability which the doctors could not find on enlistment actually existed then.
This was one of the points which the Legion emphasized when it appeared before the cabinet on November 10 of last year. At that time the Legion recommended that section 13 (1) (a) of the Pension Act be amended so that, where a pension applicant who served in an actual theatre of war is found to have a disability resulting from an injury or a disease not recorded on medical examination prior to enlistment, such injury or disease shall be presumed to have occurred or had its inception subsequent to an enlistment. There seems to be no good reason why that amendment should not be written into the Pension Act.
Another necessary change is to do away with the deadline against the marriage of a veteran which took place on or after the first of May, 1954. As the law stands at the present time, a veteran contracting such a marriage cannot get any allowance for his wife, and if he dies his widow can get no pension unless they were married before the


first of May, 1954. The reason a deadline was written into the Pension Act in the first place was the fear that when Canadian veterans grew old they might be picked up by some young lady of 20 or 21 who was looking forward to getting a pension for the rest of her life. That was the basis upon which the deadline was written into the act. I do not think it ever had any justification in fact because the pension commission has always been given very wide discretion in such cases. If the veteran had not a reasonable expectation of life for a period of one year, then the pension commission has the power to refuse to grant the pension. Surely this change should be made now.
It is very significant that there is no such deadline in the War Veterans Allowance Act. I refer to the booklet on war veterans allowances which states that the widow of a veteran who died within one year of the date of his marriage shall be ineligible for the war veterans allowance unless it is considered that at the time of his marriage the veteran had a reasonable life expectancy of at least one year. A similar provision should be sufficient in the case of the Pension Act. Strange to say, there is a provision in the Pension Act that if the veteran has been living with a woman, although not married to her, before the deadline date, and marries her afterwards he can get the payment for a wife and she qualifies for payment as a widow; but otherwise if the veteran marries after the deadline date he cannot get any allowance for his wife and if he dies his widow can get no pension. It really is a ridiculous situation. I know some cases where very great hardship has been suffered as the result of the deadline, and I think it should be removed entirely.
The Legion has also advocated that there should be a change with regard to the date from which a pension can be paid. At the present time there is a restriction. Once the pension is granted it is not necessarily retroactive to the date on which the application for pension was made. It is true that power is given to the pension commission to make a six months retroactive award if the delay has caused hardship and distress and a further 18 months retroactive award where there are certain delays and administrative difficulties beyond the applicant's control. In an editorial in the March issue of The Legionary I find the Legion stating, and they should know, that the commission rarely recognizes the existence of such special circumstances. The editorial goes on to say:
It is particularly interesting to note that no provision whatsoever is made for the correction of

an error on the part of the commission or any departmental doctor or official. If an error has been committed, the pensioner must remain the loser.
That situation, Mr. Chairman, is not good enough, and I believe that provision should be made for payment of the pension from the date of application.
The final problem which should have been met this year in connection with the Pension Act is the amount that can be paid to dependent parents. These are cases in which the veteran has lost his life. The pension commission is given power to make payments to a dependent parent or even to two parents if there should be a need. At the present time they can get only $75 a month for one parent and $100 a month for two. The Legion has recommended that these payments should be increased to $100 per month for one parent and $125 per month for two. If that were done, those figures would be in line with the figures for other pensions of a similar nature. Formerly the same figure applied all round and I do not see why the distinction was made when the Pension Act was revised.
Those are some of the problems, Mr. Chairman, facing the veterans of Canada today. Of course, there are others; but certainly those particular problems should have been dealt with this session. That brings me back to my earlier statement that there is a need now to attack veterans problems with renewed vigour and to get away from this tendency to think that everything is lovely and that we no longer need to do anything about the veteran or his dependents.
The place for action primarily is right here in parliament. The responsibility to these veterans and their dependents rests here on the members of the Canadian parliament. I suggest that we must see to it that Canadian veterans and their dependents who made such sacrifices for this nation not only shall not be neglected at the present time but shall never be forgotten.

Mr. Chairman, following the hon. member for Vancouver-Quadra I would be among the first to assert that certainly there are still veterans problems to be solved in this country. Despite the magnificent job the Department of Veterans Affairs is doing,
I do not suppose all of those problems will ever be solved. However, I maintain that the department is doing a terrific job, that it is gradually whittling down those problems and solving them, and that it is making our veterans affairs administration the best of any country in the world.
Yesterday in the Ottawa Journal there was an extremely interesting article which I believe bears me out on this particular theme.
Supply-Veterans Affairs It was written by Walter Gilhooly under the heading "The Ottawa Scene". It mentions two veterans, by name, Dave Polowin, and Lou Mirsky. Polowin was an air gunner with 425 R.C.A.F. Alouette Squadron. Mirsky was in the R.C.O.C. and third division. These two veterans apparently have started a rather unique delicatessen down on Elgin street. This article mentions their experiences following the war. I should just like to bring to your attention, Mr. Chairman, a little bit of this experience as one of them describes it. He states:
I came back from overseas in 1946 and all that I had was the uniform on my back and the government owned that . . . Lou Mirsky wasn't much better off. We had, of course, our re-establishment credits and our war service gratuities. You should have seen this place-
This refers to their delicatessen.
-when we started-a regular hole-in-the-wall. Three of us ran the joint-Lou and me and one employee. Now we employ 14 workers, and it costs us 50, 60 thousand a year to run the place.
Here is the part that I want to emphasize.
D.V.A. fixed us up.
That is the Department of Veterans Affairs.
They helped us finance and they guaranteed us salaries for six months in case the place didn't pay enough to keep us. D.V.A. gave Canadian troops the best deal any troops in the world got after the war.
I believe that is quite true, Mr. Chairman. I only want to add that I am quite certain that the majority or, in fact, practically all of the veterans in my particular area around Durham constituency feel exactly the same way, namely that they have been given a remarkably fine deal, and they have great respect for the Department of Veterans Affairs in all of its activities.

Mr. Chairman, I rise to make a few remarks in this, as I suppose you might call it, most inspiring atmosphere. I must say that last Friday I listened with a great deal of interest to the minister's review of the activities of his department during the past year. Since listening to it,
I reread his speech. I think there was some quite interesting information in his remarks. However, before going on to the few things I wish to say I must express my appreciation of the courtesy of the minister, the Canadian pension commission, the war veterans allowance board, the senior officials in Ottawa and the district officials in British Columbia, for the kindness and courtesy they have always extended to me when I have had occasion to place my troubles in their laps. I must say that their kindness and prompt attention to any of the problems I have had to bring to their attention have certainly assisted me better to represent my veteran constituents.

Supply-Veterans Affairs
I think it is only fair, Mr. Chairman, that I should not omit the lady members of the senior staff. I have occasion to see them occasionally. Their charm, kindness, sympathy, understanding and knowledge is appreciated, I know, by a good many members of this house. I am sure it is quite safe to say that their knowledge, tact and kindness frequently acts as oil on the creaking wheels of administrative machinery. With others, I must say how much many of us regret the passing of Dr. A. P. Warner some time ago. I think it is only fair to say that, in his passing, the veterans lost a very good friend indeed. I want to mention the retirement of Brigadier Topp from the Canadian pension commission. He will be missed by many in this house and outside of it. I wish to make reference to the retirement of Mr. George Derby as western regional administrator on May 12 of this year after, I understand, 37J years of service with the department or its predecessors. I first met Mr. Derby in Shaughnessy hospital in 1918 and I have known him since that time. I am sure there are many veterans in British Columbia and in western Canada who will have reason to remember his services in the department with gratitude and affection. I am sure there are thousands who will wish him a long and happy retirement.
Mr. Chairman, in listening to the minister I was very glad to hear of the review of
3.000	cases of pensioners whose disabilities were from 40 per cent to 45 per cent and to know that, as a result of that review, a substantial number of those veterans are now receiving a 50 per cent pension or more. Figures do not mean much to the general public in a case like that; but any one who has been closely connected with and interested in veterans affairs knows what a great deal it means to these veterans and their dependents whose pensions are now raised to 50 per cent or above.
I am very glad to know that the pension commission undertook that review. I was also pleased to hear of the review of the
6.000	cases of pensioners suffering from deafness or defective hearing, and that over half those pensioners will benefit as the result of this review. I was also glad to note that the department is adopting a more liberal policy toward dependent parents.
Another point the minister mentioned which was of interest to me was that over
3.000	adopted children are now receiving additional pensions. These things together do indicate an active and continuing concern on the part of the minister and his officials with these veterans and their problems.

As far as this committee is concerned, there has been one major achievement to the advantage of veterans this session, in my [DOT] opinion; that is the making public of the table of disabilities, which the Legion has urged for many years. This session my attention was particularly focused on this question as a result of reading an article written by Adam W. Williams, chairman of the pensions, treatment and W.V.A. committee of the British Columbia command of the Legion. He dealt with the facts very well indeed and the need for the publication of this table.
I must give major credit to the British Columbia command of the Canadian Legion for bringing this question to the attention of hon. members and others. I think it is quite correct to say that the British Columbia command, as the minister has known on occasions, is one of the most aggressive commands in Canada, and it is staffed with some very alert and active officers.
Before passing from this subject I must pay a tribute to Bob Macnicol, who has been closely associated with the Legion and the great war veterans' activities in British Columbia, and has done such excellent work.
I think it is only fair to give credit to those people who have given such good service and, as far as Mr. Macnicol is concerned, since his retirement a great deal of voluntary service and time. This was a matter of some importance because I have heard it discussed at the Legion meetings; I have discussed it with veterans' advocates, and I have discussed it with officials of the Canadian Legion in British Columbia.
When I read the article I began to think just what could be done to ferret this out. I had a discussion with the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre. I said to him, "I have a good notion to put a resolution on the order paper so we can have a debate on this specific question." He said, "Well, why not put a motion for production of papers?" I am one to pick other people's brains on occasions, and I immediately seized on the suggestion and placed a motion on the order paper for the production of papers. I am very glad indeed that the minister, after consideration, saw fit to allow that motion to be adopted unanimously by the house. Since then I have heard from a number of Legion officials, not in Ottawa, and from branches and from two or three veterans' advocates who said that to date it has been of considerable advantage to a number of veterans.
In concluding his remarks the minister also was frank enough to indicate that he considered that possibly some amendments were still necessary to veterans' legislation. That indicated he had an open mind and I am quite sure, being in that state of mind, he will listen

most sympathetically to any representations made by the Canadian Legion or hon. members.
The 16th dominion convention of the Canadian Legion was held recently in Vancouver, and this parliament of the Canadian veterans adopted a number of resolutions. The majority of those resolutions dealt with war veterans allowances, the Pension Act, the Veterans' Land Act, and resolutions that have come before the dominion convention of the Canadian Legion on a number of occasions. They are the hard core problems which the legion wishes the government to solve by necessary amendments to legislation. I am not going to deal in detail with those resolutions. The hon. member for Royal and the hon. member for Vancouver-Quadra mentioned them. I am simply going to mention them. I am not going to take the time of the committee to tell the minister what he already knows, but the veterans I represent asked me to support any suggestions in this respect and to bring their interest in this matter to the attention of the minister and his officials.
From my contact with veterans I think the most pressing problem is an amendment to the War Veterans Allowance Act that would raise the ceiling on permissive income so it would be $1,200 for single men and $2,000 for married men. From personal experience I know that would be a great help to a good number of veterans in this country. I say it is the most pressing problem and possibly the first problem in the minds of the greatest number of veterans. As a result of attending Legion meetings and discussing it with people in my constituency and in other places, I do most heartily support representations made in that respect. The Legion indicated its continuing interest in that matter even as late as March of this year, in an editorial in The Legionary.
I also want to support the plea on behalf of those veterans of the first world war who served in England only. They should receive the war veterans allowance. They are growing fewer and fewer in numbers. I am sure it would not be a great expense. The present circumstances are somewhat unjust and unfair for reasons mentioned by the hon. member for Royal and by four other hon. members.
It just happened that a veteran stayed in England. I know a veteran in my company who just before we left for France was transferred to the pay office and did his best to get out of it. He was an accountant, so he went to the pay office and stayed in London for the rest of the war. Another veteran went to France and stayed at Havre working

Supply-Veterans Affairs around the camp. He gets the war veterans allowance. Really there was no possible difference in risk between staying in London in the pay office and staying in Havre working around the camp, both doing what they were told to do as soldiers. I do support the representations made on behalf of those veterans.
I also support the representations made on behalf of widows of veterans who now have 20 years' residence in Canada. As one who is interested in this, I must at this point mention the work done by the ladies of the non-pensioned widows' association. I also want to compliment the parliamentary assistant on his special and particular interest in this problem. I know he has been very kind to this group of ladies when they have visited Ottawa, and I know he pays particular attention to their problems'.
My final appeal with respect to the war veterans allowance I have mentioned several times in recent years. It has to do with veterans who have to reside outside of Canada for health reasons and who obtain a certificate from a departmental doctor to prove it. They should continue to receive the war veterans allowance. They are very few in number indeed. I know from my personal experience of one very unfortunate case. Under the present law and regulations nothing can be done for this man; consequently he is now living in Mexico as the result of a fund which is being organized and to which his veteran friends contribute every month. I think they manage to send about $50 a month to him in Mexico City, and I am very happy to chip in my little bit to help out.
I also think there should be the few minor amendments to the Pension Act with respect to dependent parents that have been suggested by the Canadian Legion. Compared to what has been done these are minor amendments, and I urge the minister and the government to give consideration to them. That is all I have to say concerning the War Veterans Allowance Act and the Pension Act. Now I want to say a word with respect to the Veterans' Land Act.
First of all I must say the local administration so far as I can see is excellent, that part of it of which I have knowledge. The officials with whom I deal in my constituency are competent and always willing to try to deal with any particular problem to the advantage of the veteran according to the law and regulation. However, in my constituency there are over 200 veterans, particularly young married veterans, who are unable to take advantage of the small holding section of the Veterans' Land Act because of the acreage required. I know the minister looks at me as

Supply-Veterans Affairs if to say this is a boring topic and one which I have mentioned before, but this is a serious problem for veterans in a country with topography like ours where there are mountains, lakes and valleys and where it is not easy to obtain two or three acres of land. Most of these men are working in the mining industry or the lumber industry. A quarter of an acre is a quite sufficient area for a small holding for any man working in industry, and I suggest that further consideration be given to these particular circumstances and the regulations so amended that a veteran can obtain a holding as small in area as one quarter of an acre.
I think there is general recognition of the good work being done by the Veterans' Land Act administration. I have received one general criticism, not of the particular officials of Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation concerned nor of any' individual, but for some reason or another veterans like to come under the administration of the Department of Veterans Affairs. It is a department with a head and a heart-some have considerable head but not very much heart-and I find it is the almost unanimous wish of veterans who have to build houses that the administration of all housing in which veterans are concerned remain within the jurisdiction of the Veterans' Land Act administration.
The Department of Veterans Affairs, Mr. Chairman, is spending about $245 million this year. Changing conditions and circumstances create new problems almost from day to day for the veterans, the dependents of veterans, the administration and the government. In our opinion a standing committee on veterans affairs is necessary if parliament is going to deal effectively and with fairness with all the human beings concerned.
I know that the area in which we can tackle the government with respect to veterans affairs is somewhat circumscribed. We have certain particular problems that are not settled. We will have other problems that will arise in the days to come, and that is why we think it is essential that there should be a standing parliamentary committee on veterans affairs. It would provide an opportunity for representations to be made by veterans' organizations. It would provide an opportunity for the hearing of evidence from the departmental officials and a resume of their activities, and would give us a better understanding of the administration of the affairs of the department. It would provide for an annual review of veterans' legislation as the result of listening to representations made by veterans' organizations, for amendments and improvements, and it would provide the


committee, in addition, an opportunity to make recommendations to the government as a result of these representations, this evidence, this hearing of the officials and as a result of the personal experience of the members concerned.
The request for a standing committee on veterans affairs is genuine and has been voiced from this side of the house and by some hon. members on the other side for some years. I think the need is obvious if we are going to serve the veteran to the best advantage. All that is required is recognition of that need and recognition of the facts by this government.
That is all I am going to say on the estimates at this time. I may have some comments to make under particular items, but at this point I shall conclude my remarks.

Mr. Chairman, it was just
about a year ago that we started to discuss the estimates of the Department of Veterans Affairs during last session. During the course of my remarks at that time I commented upon the fact that the Minister of Veterans Affairs for five years in succession had failed to make any statement at the beginning of his estimates. I did not think he would accept my advice which I tendered to him on that occasion, but to my astonishment he came forward this year and made a statement at the opening of his estimates.
That is an encouraging advance, and if the minister has charge of this department on some other occasion I hope he will continue that practice, because it is essential that a minister should review the work of the year and place it before the committee. Of course when I examine his statement made just a few days ago I find there are many omissions, but I am going to be patient and generous with him and hope for improvement as we go along.
I do not propose during the course of my remarks today to offer any criticism of the work of the officials of the Department of Veterans Affairs. I think within the limitations of the act and the limitations of the direction given to them they are doing an efficient piece of work but, if necessary, I do propose to be critical of the actions of the minister and the ineffectiveness of the legislation as I see it.
The minister pointed out that no legislation was introduced this year and seemed to imply by that remark that everything was all right. That struck me as being rather odd, because last year the estimates of this department went before the estimates committee of the House of Commons and a fairly exhaustive study of the Department of Veterans Affairs

was carried out in that committee. Various officials appeared before us and gave the committee all the information that was asked for and disclosed to us that they are as efficient as any members of the civil service. During the course of that comprehensive study of this department last year several points came up which I thought would be reviewed in the interval, and I expected that the minister would comment on them at this time.
In the estimates committee we went into the subject of the rates of pension with considerable care. Facts and figures were produced. For perhaps the first time the pension commission in the person of the chairman appeared before us and gave a great deal of information with regard to disability pensions. I thought we indicated to the minister at that time, and subsequently when the estimates came before the committee of the whole house, that the pension rates were not entirely satisfactory.
We get the same thing in connection with war veterans allowances. We went into that and pointed out the alterations that should be made to improve war veterans allowances. We discussed at considerable length the benefit of doubt section in the veterans' charter, yet nothing is said about it this year by the minister. We discussed at considerable length section 13 (2) of the Pension Act which provides for the granting of pensions to veterans or dependents where the veteran has suffered injury or death in connection with a disability which arose out of or was directly connected with his military service. That section has been a stumbling block for a number of years in connection with the granting of pensions. It was discussed thoroughly by the committee which sat last year, but it is passed by without any comment by the minister this year.
We discussed also the question of pensions for men who served in England in the first world war, but it passes without comment this year. We discussed at some length in the estimates committee and again in the house last year the problems of our veterans. We urged the setting up of a standing committee on veterans affairs, but again no result.
That is not good enough. There was a much more exhaustive study last year of the affairs of the Department of Veterans Affairs than we have had in previous years. The officials were there to be examined and to answer our questions. Problems which required rectification were brought to the attention of the minister. Yet the minister informs us that there is to be no legislation brought down this year, which gives the impression that everything is fine with regard to veterans
Supply-Veterans Affairs affairs. Consequently we are placed once again in the position of having to draw to the attention of the minister the fact that everything is not right with veterans affairs. Some changes need to be made and should have been made long ago. They can still be made. Just a few minutes ago the hon. member for Durham was telling us how wonderful the veterans' charter was, and he quoted from a newspaper to the effect that members of the forces had benefited greatly after the conclusion of the last war from the assistance they had received.
That is all very well, but it should be placed against what is contained in the departmental report of 1955, the last one that is available to us. That indicates that 5,305 veterans of world war I made application to the pension commission for decisions of one sort or another. The same report contains the information that disability pensioners of world war I made application to the pension commission for additional or other allowances to the number of 1,543. Similar information with regard to world war II shows that in 1954-55 veterans of that war made 8,873 applications to the Canadian pension commission. If everything were perfectly all right with regard to veterans legislation we would not have applications of that nature coming before the pension commission at this stage, certainly not from veterans of world war I. It is quite obvious that the situation is not quite as rosy as some people attempt to make out.
As I pointed out to the house last year, and as I repeat this year, a fairly exhaustive study indicates that the picture with regard to those who are on pension is not particularly satisfactory. The chairman of the pension commission gave figures to show that in the case of world war I pensioners, those receiving a pension of 50 per cent or better constituted only 25 per cent of the total number. Three-quarters of world war I pensioners are receiving pensions of less than 50 per cent, and the average pension is $32.64.
World war II pensioners receiving pensions of 50 per cent or more constitute 17 per cent of the total, and 83 per cent are receiving pensions of under 50 per cent. The average pension for world war II pensioners is $24.52. It is quite evident from those figures that the Canadian pension scheme is not particularly generous. If it were a generous scheme, how does it come about that 10,000 disability pensioners have to receive additional assistance by way of war veterans allowances or other assistance plans?
Things are not as satisfactory as some people would try to persuade us, and much more

It is for that and other reasons that we keep asking for a standing committee on veterans affairs where matters such as this could be reviewed. Otherwise things are likely to be taken for granted. As I have pointed out, the work of the pension commission did not come under detailed review until last year, before the estimates committee; at least not for a number of years. The facts and figures which I have given emerged from that review.
A standing committee meeting every year would be able to receive representations from veterans organizations, would be able to interview the officials of the department, and could keep closely in touch with the veteran situation throughout the country. We must remember that this is a continuing problem. It is safe to say that for 70 years after any war there will be problems concerning the veterans of that particular war. The figures shown in the departmental report indicate that the ages of world war I veterans run from 50 to 99 years. Those who are in their fifties on that disability list may live until they are 99; thus you could have another 40-odd years in which you would have to deal with disability pensioners of world war I. The ages of pensioners of world war II run from 25 to something in the sixties, so there will be a long period ahead in which problems affecting veterans of world war II will have to be considered. We are not going to get rid of the problems facing our veterans for a long time, and we must settle down and accept the fact that we have to look after the veterans of wars in which Canada has been engaged. Don't forget that the South African veterans are still with us. So for those reasons and others a standing committee on veterans affairs is the proper thing to set up. There too we would discover some of the reasons why there are so many thousands of applications for pensions being made even at the present time by world war I veterans. We might be able to find out why so many of those applications are brought forward and why so many of them are turned down.
May I point out to the minister, and he may pass the word along to his officials- and this is the only criticism I am making of the officials-that it is about time they altered a sentence in their departmental report. I think I drew it to their attention last year. If I did not I do so now, and if I did I repeat it. In the report in 1951, and it is repeated in the reports of 1953, 1954


and now in 1955, words like this appear in reference to applications for pensions:
In all cases, every effort is made to obtain final settlement without recourse to an appeal board-
I worked out the figures and discovered that despite all those efforts, 91-2 per cent of all first and second hearings failed. So I think the sentence is completely meaningless. It occurs in the report for 1955 with the additional phrase added:
-and in many instances finality is reached by this means.
That does not happen. Most of these applications fall to the ground on first and second hearings despite all these efforts. I think a standing committee on veterans affairs might investigate that particular problem and see whether anything could be done about it.
I am not going to cover the ground that has already been touched on by other members on this side of the house, but I certainly am in complete sympathy with the veterans' organizations that continue to press for attention with regard to disability pensioners, that continue to press for attention to the War Veterans Allowance Act and the regulations thereunder, and that continue to press for increased financial assistance to war veterans. I am not going to touch on the question of casual earnings; that comes up every year. It has been mentioned here again this year, and the veterans' organization continue to draw it to our attention. These are problems that are pressing; they affect individuals many of whom are in desperate circumstances.
It is certainly not right for anyone to attempt to create the impression that everything is all right with regard to veterans affairs in Canada and that there is a great charter which looks after all the veterans. My investigation shows that that is not so. I am not going to repeat the figures I used last year, when I dealt with this at some length and indicated that thousands of veterans have not received any assistance whatsoever since the first world war, and the same is going to be true of veterans of the second world war. Many thousands, of course, have not asked for assistance, but it struck me as very odd when I looked into it last year that half the number of those who had been wounded in the first great war had not been placed on the pension roll, and it strikes me as odd at the present time that men are getting pensions now, 40 years after the first world war, for gunshot wounds suffered then.
I noted that the minister referred to a review made of about 3,000 pensioners who were receiving disability pensions of 40 per cent and 45 per cent. He stated the other day that a very substantial number of these awards were increased to 50 per cent and

more, making their dependents eligible for an award in the event of death. I had hoped there would be a table in the 1955 report indicating that activity-it may be there and I have not found it-or that the minister would give us the exact figures and not merely the statement that a very substantial number of these awards were increased. Why not pin it down and let us have the actual number, and give us the percentage of those who now get 50 per cent or more pension so we may make a proper comparison?
I think it would not hurt at all for a standing committee on veterans affairs to examine the matter I raised last year in the estimates committee and mentioned in the house, that a ceiling seems to have been set on the amount of money available for pensions over the years. I have traced the course of these for 20 years. There seems to be a ceiling, and as men die others can be added to the pension roll. Why did it not happen that a few years after the first world war the number on pension went away up to a high figure and then declined, instead of running almost level for a long period? I asked the question in regard to the second world war. Why should not the pension roll for the second world war have mounted very rapidly and then soon started to decline? If you look at the record you will find that there is a sort of dead level for 25 years, and that year after year men are being placed on the pension roll.
The only conclusion I can draw is that some ceiling has been set over all these years for these pensions, and as 800 or 1,000 men die each year, the pension board can receive applications from and consider adding to the pension roll 800 or 1,000 men, so the financial obligation remains the same. A standing committee could look into that as well as other things.
I have some other remarks on the Department of Veterans Affairs to be made later.

Mr. Chairman, at this time I wish to record my support for a number of suggestions relative to veterans' legislation. This afternoon we listened to the hon. member for Durham congratulating the department on the splendid achievements of the past, and he made some remarks relative to the widespread satisfaction that exists with regard to the legislation as we now have it. I am sure that none of us believe that every problem has been taken care of and solved, but I may say that all veterans and those who are interested in veterans affairs are appreciative of what has been done. Nevertheless, I think they will take at face value the implications in the minister's speech the other day, when he made the remark that further amendments would be possible in the future.
Supply-Veterans Affairs Certainly we shall be looking forward to the introduction of some of those amendments, and we hope it is going to be in the not too distant future.
The hon. member for Vancouver-Quadra, in speaking this afternoon, made the statement that some of these problems would be solved when the Progressive Conservative party forms the government. I certainly hope we do not have to wait that long, because if that is so there will be a great many more opportunities to raise some of these very same problems in the future. However, we hope that as the days go by the minister and his department will give serious and favourable consideration to many of the subjects that have been raised in the course of this debate.
It has been indicated that one of the main problems faced by the veterans and those interested in veterans affairs is the matter of the permissive income. In reading the speech the minister made when introducing his departmental estimates I noticed that he referred to the significant change that had been made in the War Veterans Allowance Act last year with reference to the rates and the ceilings. Prior to the introduction last year of the legislation to which the minister referred we had hopes that he would be prepared to meet the requests of the Legion and the other veterans' organizations with respect to permissive income. However, when the legislation was introduced, we were disappointed to find that he had only gone part way. Perhaps it was just meant to appease those who had been persistent in their requests for increases. However, whatever the reason the department did not see fit to go all the way and grant the requests that the permissive ceiling be raised to $1,200 for single recipients and $2,000 for married recipients.
I think some satisfaction was taken in the view that these increases had taken care of the situation to a large extent. When we think of the entire picture and consider those who have the opportunity to supplement their allowance or income by casual earnings, perhaps such recipients are in a fair position; but then we are also reminded of the fact that there are those who are not in a position to take advantage of the casual earnings clause. There are those who are not physically able. There are those who are unable because of the economic situation in their communities. They do not have the privilege of supplementing their income, and we find they are still in a very difficult financial position. I think the minister and his department should give serious consideration to that particular class.

Another group to whom references have been made during the course of the debate are the veterans who are residing outside of Canada. I raised this same matter with respect to old age pension recipients. I felt that they should not be disqualified if for some particular reason, health or otherwise, they were required or desired to live outside of Canada. Certainly I feel just as strongly in the case of veterans who, for health or perhaps other reasons, want to live outside of Canada. I do not see why they should be disqualified so far as the war veterans allowance is concerned.
I know this matter has also been brought to the attention of the minister and the department not only during the course of this debate but on other occasions, and also by the Canadian Legion and the other veterans' organizations. I trust it is still under consideration. If not, I hope the minister and his department will take it under advisement and give serious consideration to this particular matter having to do with veterans' legislation.
There is another request to which I should like to give my support. I refer to the request on behalf of the widows of those who served in the allied forces during the first war and whose husbands died before they had fulfilled the 20-year residence qualification entitling them to the war veterans allowance. I believe this matter has also been given consideration by the department, but for some reason or other they have not seen fit to accede to the request. I suggest that the recommendation that when the widow has fulfilled the 20-year residence qualification she should be qualified to receive the allowance is valid and fair, and I would suggest that this recommendation be given consideration and the request acceded to.
There is another matter to which I referred last year during the debate on veterans affairs, and I believe it has also been referred to today. It has to do with those veterans who served in England during the first world war but did not get to the actual scene of battle. Last year when I spoke I referred to the fact that I had not been aware that during the first world war even those in England were subjected to enemy attack and bombardment. I think that should qualify them to receive the war veterans allowance, because I imagine there may have been some, perhaps not many, who crossed the channel, set foot in France and yet were not subjected to even the same degree of attack and bombardment as these men in England were on some occasions. It has also been indicated that the conditions in England under which these veterans were required to live were 

difficult, and this fact certainly should warrant some consideration of the matter. Again, their service in England may have been more arduous than in the case of some of those who perhaps just landed in France and did not actually go into a theatre of combat.
While discussing veterans affairs with veterans' leaders in my own constituency one particular matter was drawn to my attention, and I want to pass it along to the minister at this time. It is the request that consideration be given to providing medical services, drugs, etc., to the wives of war veterans allowance recipients. I feel this is a request which should be given serious consideration. I know this matter has also been raised before and drawn to the attention of the department; nevertheless up to the present favourable action has not been taken in relation to the request.
These are some of the matters to which I should like to draw attention. Perhaps they have all been mentioned before. It has been suggested today that some of these problems have been brought to the attention of the house and the department on many occasions, that they have been contained in briefs submitted by the Canadian Legion and other veterans' organizations. It may be that the department feels there are justifiable reasons why the requests should not or cannot be granted, but I certainly feel that until these requests are met and the problems are solved we should not be too ready to settle back and take the attitude that the veterans' charter covers all the problems that confront our veterans in this day and age.
In introducing his estimates the minister referred to the fact that with the exception of one minor amendment to the Veterans Business and Professional Loans Act, no veterans' legislation was to be introduced at this session. I trust that is not an indication that no further pressing problems are evident, and that we can settle back and take a breathing spell and perhaps review the situation again in the years that lie ahead. These matters call for urgent consideration.
The request has been made that a standing committee on veterans affairs be set up. I think I have heard the same request made in the past three sessions during which I have served in the House of Commons. I have also seen this subject referred to in the various veterans' periodicals. However, so far the government has not seen fit to set up such a committee. Last year a special committee was established to deal with veterans' legislation that would be referred to it. I know we appreciated the setting up of that committee last year, but even at that time we indicated that we felt it was not adequate

for the needs because of the fact that the terms of reference were limited to those matters which had been referred to it by the house. This session we have not even had a committee set up in this session.
I think this is another indication that perhaps we are kind of settling back as far as the veterans' legislation and the veterans' problems are concerned. I certainly hope that favourable consideration will be given to the setting up of a committee and that the request that has been made on so many occasions in this regard will be acceded to.
So, Mr. Chairman, I call attention to these problems, I give my support to the request for a solution to them, and I trust that the minister and his department will give serious and favourable consideration to each and every one of them.

Mr. Chairman, I have no intention of unduly delaying the passing of any of these items, but I think I should make some comment on some of the statements made from the opposite side of the house today and one statement made by the hon. member for New Westminster the other day.
While I generally agree with what my good friend the hon. member for Winnipeg South Centre said, I thought he made one most unfortunate suggestion, and one which certainly will do the cause of the veterans in Canada no over-all good, when he suggested that there was some kind of sinister thing like an over-all ceiling on expenditures and therefore new applicants could be taken on the list as pensioners only as the old ones die off, or something to that effect.
When that suggestion was made, I think last year, I discussed this rather remarkable proposition with some of the responsible officials. I found, of course, that they were highly incensed at the implication or insinuation that there could be anything of this kind because it was, to a certain extent, a challenge to their integrity. I think it is obviously true that of all the departments in this government, there is no department of government where the officials from the top to the bottom give more faithful and fairer service to this house and to the people of Canada than do the officials of that particular department.
On reflection I think my good friend the hon. member for Winnipeg South Centre will realize that, while it is a very melancholy thought, any good statistician can figure out in advance how many of us "old sweats" are going to die off every particular year. I think nobody but the Lord God Almighty himself can tell whether the hon. member for Winnipeg South Centre or the hon. member for Vancouver South is going to be with us
Supply-Veterans Affairs next year; but I think any good statistician can say how many of the veterans of world war I, of age 60 to 70, are going to be with us one year from now, how many are going to be with us five years from now, how many are going to be with us 10 years from now and so on down the list.
I therefore think it is quite obvious that the statisticians of the department always know in advance just what the trend is; and I believe the implication is most unfair that they are slanting their judicial decision as to the eligibility of applicants according to the amount of extra money that might be made available from "old sweats" passing to their reward.
Then with regard to some of the remarkable misstatements made by some of the members of the opposition, I thought also that my good friend the hon. member for New Westminster was certainly on false ground the other day when he suggested this. I forget how he put it, but it was to the effect that the British Columbia government had a grievance against the federal government for not giving free treatment to war veterans allowance recipients. Mr. Chairman, everybody in British Columbia including the people on war veterans allowance is forced to pay the 5 per cent compulsory sales tax which is collected for free hospital treatment.
No, it is not. It is 2 per cent.

If we are going to charge to the people what they ought to pay to the federal government, the government of Canada should be presenting a hospital bill to the Social Credit government of British Columbia every year to make up for the free hospital treatment that is given the veterans allowance patients in federal hospitals, for which not a single cent is charged to the Social Credit government of British Columbia.
Put the record straight. It is 2 per cent, not 5 per cent.

It is 5 per cent over-all. All we know is who pays it and how much. I think it is a very poor suggestion for the hon. member for New Westminster to make, especially when the same Social Credit government of British Columbia will not even make eligible for hospital services the incoming dependents of the people in the armed services until after they have lived in British Columbia for so many months. I think it is a year or so many months additional.

I think they tried to work it out with the federal government, did they not?
