It takes two to make an agreement.
That is the trouble.

I think they had better start. To concentrate now on the happier side, I cannot agree either with some of my hon. friends opposite that there have been no improvements in the general set-up. I know this if my own mail bag is any criterion, and I think I probably get as much mail as most members of this house. I know that in the first year of this parliament my mail ran to over 1,000 letters per month asking for increases in the war veterans allowance, for the raising of ceilings on casual earnings and so on. This year I do not think I have had four letters from my constituents on the general question of increases or anything to do with the general set-up of the war veterans' system. I have had some letters of the other kind.
I remember one of the first modest things I tried to do when I came to this house, apart from doing what other members on both sides of the house were doing, namely trying to get increases in war veterans allowances which we subsequently succeeded in getting. I remember that one of the first letters I wrote was to the present minister.
May I interject here for just a moment, Mr. Chairman, that I have heard some rather ridiculous talk from the other side of the house about wanting a full-time minister. Our minister is a two-handed minister, quite capable of carrying two jobs at once. If the time ever came when he was not able to carry out one job with each hand, I know which job would be given up. The Prime Minister would be looking for a new postmaster general, because the veterans of Canada are smart enough to know that they have the most friendly and co-operative of all the distinguished ministers who have held this distinguished post. None has had a greater and more deserved hold on the affections of the veterans of Canada than has the hon. gentleman who sits in that position today and who is too modest to say so himself.
May I mention one of the relatively small things which we sometimes find pay big dividends. I remember almost the first day I got in this House of Commons-certainly in the first week or month-taking up the question of making adopted children eligible along with natural children for the allowances drawn by veterans. This year we saw in the report that several thousand of these children are now drawing those allowances.
Sometimes when we think of it in terms of how much it costs the country we may be


inclined to forget the human equation. I have a letter in my file from a very fine war veteran in British Columbia who has a couple of children of his own and three adopted children of rather mixed parentage, perhaps. I remember both that man and his wife telling me that they were not so much interested in the actual allowance they would draw for those adopted children, but it was the idea that they could tell those children that the government of Canada had just as high a regard for them as it had for the natural children born in the ordinary course of the marriage relationship. Perhaps some of these small things are just as important in human terms as some of the spectacular things about which we all hear.
One other thing in the report this year that certainly warmed my heart was that somebody-I do not know who was responsible; perhaps it was a combined effort-took it upon himself or themselves to review the assessment of all the disability pensioners in the 40 per cent and 45 per cent disability group. We all know, Mr. Chairman, the practical effect of that was to make eligible for widows' pensions, when the unhappy occurrence takes place that the husband passes on and the wife remains, several thousand Canadian women who were not eligible until that general over-all revision.
While I do not think, Mr. Chairman, there is anyone certainly on this side of the house who is going to be inclined to rest on the laurels of our pension legislation, I certainly do not think we have anything to be ashamed of. I remember just about a week or so ago reading a long account in the New York Times of the discussion in the congress of the United States of the proposed revisions in their pension system, and it certainly gave me a thrill to read that even after all these years the United States has nothing that can remotely compare with the system we have in Canada with respect to disability pensions and war veterans allowances. After all these years the great rich United States, by far the richest country in the whole world, is only now coming around to propose, if you please, a very moderate and limited form of system which we have had ever since 1930 in our war veterans allowance legislation in this country. When I say we have had it ever since 1930 I mean we have had it by reason of the support that veterans' reforms have always received from all sides of the house.
I am not going to close my little talk today without making some practical suggestions. I believe we should have a select veterans' committee of this house meeting more often.

I certainly hope there is a veterans' committee next year if we get a chance to set it up. In any event, there are certain things we were not able to bring to finality at the last session of the veterans' committee which I personally would like to see reconsidered. One thing in particular I would like to see reconsidered is the question of the eligibility for war veterans allowance of world war I men who served only in what is called the British theatre, especially as the people in world war II are eligible for that allowance.
It will be remembered, Mr. Chairman, that when we had our last veterans' committee at the last session of parliament, the veterans' organizations of Canada were sharply divided on this particular question. While the Canadian Legion was strongly in favour of making eligible those who had served only in England in the first world war, there were other very powerful and very widespread veterans' organizations which took a very strong position against that suggestion. I say time is marching on. In my opinion this is one subject at which we should take a second look and of which we should certainly take a more liberal view.
There is one other thing I should like to mention. I do not think any other hon. member has mentioned it so far. If he has, it must have been done when I was not able to be here. I think it was a very fine thing that the minister and the government have agreed to the proposals of the Canadian Legion and have decided to build here, on one of the finest sites in the capital of Canada, a fitting cenotaph or national memorial to the fallen of all wars.
I know, Mr. Chairman, that the beautiful memorial to the fallen of world war I which stands in Confederation square is a fine and inspiring work of art, but for various reasons it could never be transformed into a fitting memorial for the fallen of all wars. Someone pointed out to me the other day that even in its cultural aspects it is dated. I think of the gunners and their artillery horses. That was certainly all right for world war I, but I do not think the people of world war II would even know how to put the harness on the horses, let alone what to do with the spurs and so on. Therefore I think it is a very fine thing that the government has decided to yield to the suggestion of the Canadian Legion to build on one of the finest sites in the whole Dominion of Canada a fitting permanent cenotaph at which suitable ceremonies can be held from year to year.
Sometimes I think, Mr. Chairman, it would be almost worth the price if this nation would pay the fare of people across the ocean to the great battlefield of Vimy Ridge to see
Supply-Veterans Affairs what I think must be the most inspiring war memorial in the whole world today. I know that I have never looked at anything which moved me as much as did the sight of that beautiful work of art which stands on the crest of the hill dedicated forever to Canada by the grateful French nation. I think if we assign our best artists and our best sculptors to design something equally fitting for the site in Ottawa we shall have done something of which this house will always be proud and of which no Canadian need be ashamed.
Therefore, Mr. Chairman, without taking up the time of the committee any further, may I say there should be no disposition whatever for us in any part of this house to rest on our laurels in regard to veterans' legislation. What we have done is good. There are some spots in which it could be better, but we have given a fair break to the people who served this country in her hour of need.

There are just one or two matters on which I wish to comment very briefly. The first is the remarks of the minister at page 5748 of Hansard. He advised us of the review made by his department of the pensioners who were receiving 40 per cent and 45 per cent disability pensions. I should like to ask the minister whether that is the start of a review of the cases of all pensioners who receive less than 40 per cent, in the hope and expectation that physical changes that have taken place over the years will show that they are entitled to a larger pension.
The minister should be commended on what he has done in that respect, and I sincerely hope that he and the officials of his department will review the cases of all other pensioners who receive less than 40 per cent. I would also like to have the minister explain to the committee the yardstick or whatever it is that is used in establishing the percentage of disability pension of the husband to which the wife is entitled on his death. I know it is 50 per cent, but I would like the minister to explain to the committee why and how they arrived at 50 per cent, and also why the widow of a pensioner who receives a 10 per cent to 45 per cent disability pension is not entitled to at least some pension on the death of her husband.
The minister may reply that if the veteran receives a 30 per cent pension his wife would be entitled to war veterans allowance on his death and that is quite true; but as the minister knows, when the widow reaches 70 and receives the old age security pension her war veterans allowance is reduced accordingly. On the other hand if she were in receipt of a pension on account of her husband's disability she would be able to retain that and

Supply-Veterans Affairs also receive the old age security pension. I for one would be interested in having the minister tell us when he speaks how and why it has been set at 50 per cent and why his department feels that the widow of a veteran who receives less than a 50 per cent pension is not entitled to a pension on the death of her husband.
The second point which interests me is a point the minister must be tired of hearing, and that is the old question of the veteran who served only in England in world war I. On Friday last the hon. member for New Westminster read into the record an interesting letter from Mr. Garneau, chairman of the war veterans allowance board. In that letter Mr. Garneau made a most interesting statement in which he said:
... in accordance with the act, veterans of world war II who had actually left the shores of Canada before the 8th day of May, 1945, and were on their way to an actual theatre of war, may be deemed to have been on service in a theatre of actual war outside the western hemisphere.
Nobody is going to quarrel with that, Mr. Chairman, but it does seem rather far-fetched that a veteran of world war II could leave the western hemisphere, and even before reaching England, when the war was over for the purpose of the War Veterans Allowance Act he could be classed as having served in an actual theatre of war. In view of the interpretation put on the matter by the chairman of the war veterans allowance board it seems difficult to understand why the minister cannot amend the act to classify England as a theatre of war as far as world war I is concerned in relation to the War Veterans Allowance Act.
The third point with which I wish to deal was mentioned previously this afternoon by the hon. member for Kootenay West, and it is with regard to the acreage under the Veterans' Land Act. The minister and his officials must know that the price of building lots has increased considerably. Not only that, but due to the change that has taken place in the various provinces-in my own province of Ontario, for example-the tax rate has become very high and if the veteran has to have the number of acres required by the present regulations he must be penalized by paying a high tax rate each year.
For example, in the small village in which I live the average lot is one quarter of an acre in size; I think that is the standard size. A building lot would cost between $200 and $800 according to its location. The municipal tax rate this year is 80 mills. The minister can readily see that if it is necessary for the veteran to have the required number of acres he has to acquire land at a high
[Mr. White (Hastings-Frontenac) .1
price and he will be penalized each year by having to pay extremely high taxes.
The only other matter I wish to mention is with regard to the pension board. I still feel there are too many cases in which the officials are not giving the veteran the benefit of the doubt, and in far too many cases they continue to hide behind the old statement that the disability was pre-enlistment and not aggravated by war service and therefore the veteran is not pensionable. To give you an example, I have in my hand a letter written to a veteran by one of the medical officers at Sunnybrook hospital. In reporting to this veteran the doctor made the following comment:
The information regarding your findings has been forwarded to the Canadian pensions commission and I understand your claim is still under study. I would think it most likely that they will find it a pensionable disability in view of our recommendations.
This report was written by a doctor who had been in charge of this veteran for several months; but despite his report, when the matter came before the officials of the pension commission they said this was the old case of the disability being pre-enlistment and not aggravated by military service, and therefore the veteran was not pensionable. In view of that I would say to the minister that I think there must be something wrong in this particular case. An outstanding medical man wrote to the veteran setting out his views on the case, and surely he must know more about it than anyone on the pension commission. Despite this fact the old alibi concerning it being a pre-enlistment disability cropped up.
I agree wth the remarks made by the hon. member for Royal on Friday and the remarks made by the hon. member for Van-couver-Quadra this afternoon. Before I sit down I would like to emphasize again to the minister that I think he must be sufficiently satisfied, in view of the many remarks made this afternoon concerning the benefit to be derived from a veterans' committee, that he will find it possible to recommend to the government the setting up of a permanent committee on veterans affairs.

Mr. Chairman, I understand the enthusiasm shown by the hon. member for Vancouver South (Mr. Philpott) who attempted to make out that the hon. Minister of Veterans Affairs (Mr. Lapointe) is a superman by reason of the fact that he now

heads two departments in the cabinet. However, I disagree with him, because the Department of Veterans Affairs having become one of the most important in the federal administration, I believe that the minister should be relieved of his additional duties so that he may devote all his time to the department to which he had been named previously.
Mr. Chairman, under present conditions, I do not believe it is good for the country to ask any human being to head two departments in the cabinet. I hope that the right hon. Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent) will soon take steps to fill the vacancy at the Post Office Department so as to enable the present Minister of Veterans Affairs to devote all his time to those who loyally fought for peace and the defence of our territory.
I wish at this time to make a few remarks about matters which no doubt have already been mentioned but to which I want to refer again.
On behalf of veterans, I would like to urge that the ceiling on casual earnings be raised to $2,000 from the present maximum of $1,400 set for married veterans. This would seem to me only fair and reasonable, in view of the higher cost of living, that these married people be allowed an income of $2,000 a year. In the case of unmarried veterans, I believe also that it would be but fair and reasonable that the ceiling be raised from $840 to at least $1,400.
Mr. Chairman, I would like to make a correction. When I referred just now to the basic earning of married people, I should have said $1,200 and not $1,400. In fact, that was the recommendation made by the Canadian Legion to the department. I support this recommendation most wholeheartedly, and I hope that it will be taken into very serious consideration by the department concerned.
I would also like to say a word about the status of veterans who fought in the first world war, as compared to that of veterans of the second great war. Everybody knows that the war veterans allowance was granted to those first world war veterans who had served in what has been called a theatre of war. If we look at history, however, we will find that, at the end of the first world war, large numbers of soldiers were sent overseas to Europe. A certain number of them were sent to the theatre of war, which happened to be France at that time, others being sent to England, in order, no doubt, that their services could be used there. At that time
Supply-Veterans Affairs England was not considered to be a theatre of war. Now those who came back from what was then considered to be a theatre of war, that is to say France, were fortunate enough to receive an allowance from the department.
Mr. Chairman, I earnestly ask the government, at this time, to do away with what I would call this unfair discrimination between veterans of both world wars, the ones of the first war being refused the allowance granted those who served as I said a while ago, in a theatre of war.
It should not be forgotten that those who were at that time sent to England rather than to France did not choose their destination. They went because their superior officers ordered them to go. To my knowledge, no one refused to be sent either to France or to England.
I also believe, Mr. Chairman, and I think all hon. members in this house share this opinion, that veterans of the first world war had no less courage than the veterans of the last war, and that they served their country with the same loyalty as those who fought from 1939 to 1945 and also in the Korean war. Those veterans of the first world war, who for the most part are now 65 years old or more, find themselves in a painful situation, to say the least, particularly those who receive no allowance whatever.
We all know that most employers will not take on people who have reached 60, and more particularly those who are over 60, although a man of 60 is, quite often, still able to work and can sometimes do a day's work better than people much younger.
I believe that all those who fought gallantly and risked their lives in the first world war should get a more tangible mark of gratitude from the government.
It is a well known fact that from 60 to 70 is the most awkward age to get a job, since, as a rule, employers will not take on people in that age group, not for lack of sympathy but because insurance companies will not take responsibility for what might happen to those who are over 60, even when they are in the best of health and can render excellent services.
Therefore, I would ask the department, and I am speaking now on behalf of many war veterans who live in the constituency which it is my privilege to represent, that such allowance be paid in order to assist them. It is true that in the province of Quebec, at the age of 65, when one is an indigent, one may draw an allowance which enables-

So I insist that the government should look after those people even before their discharge. When a man's request for discharge has been granted, and it is definite that he will return to civilian life, the department should take the necessary steps in order to give him a chance to earn a decent living.
Now, Mr. Chairman, may I submit another suggestion? I highly appreciate the fact that the Minister of Veterans Affairs can grant, and at a very reasonable price, to war veterans who apply for it, a lot where they can build a home.
As I say, those lots are sold at a very reasonable price and are reserved for war veterans.
I wonder however if it would not be possible to extend that privilege to the widows of the veterans who gave their lives on the battlefield or who died on active service.
I would like to bring to the attention of the minister a special case which has been referred to me. This man served in both world wars, that of 1914-18 and that of 1939-45. He enlisted as a private but his gallantry, his ability and his loyalty soon gained him promotions up to the rank of colonel, which he still had when he came back from Europe in 1945, I believe. Unfortunately he died leaving a wife and children who would have liked to enjoy that same privilege of which the wife would have benefited had Providence spared him for them.
I wonder whether the department could seriously examine requests by widows of veterans in order to enable them to obtain a piece of land at a lower price and build themselves a house. Supposing a lot had been purchased last week, and that the veteran died this week, I do not believe that the department would deprive the widow of the land purchased previously.
I therefore respectfully request that this suggestion be taken into serious consideration.
